note: Magyar cavalry raids devastated East Francia repeatedly from 899 to 955, penetrating as far as Burgundy, Lorraine, Saxony, and Italy. The raids — lightning fast, burning crops and towns, returning before resistance could organize — exposed the inadequacy of Carolingian defense. The Saxon kings Henry I 'the Fowler' organized systematic counter-measures: building burgs (fortified towns), training heavy cavalry, and negotiating a 9-year truce (926–934) that bought time. His son Otto I finally crushed the Magyars at the Battle of Lechfeld (955), ending the raids and demonstrating German military superiority that enabled Otto's imperial coronation (962).

_quarry.structural_significance: Magyar raids are the central military crisis of 10th-century Germany; the raids accelerate the development of German feudal institutions (cavalry, castles, burgs); Lechfeld (955) ends the raids and establishes Otto I as the 'defender of Christendom' — the political foundation for his imperial coronation
